connection: Session 31 covered DI lifetimes. EF Core does not exist anywhere in the real practice-07092026 source -- ClockEntryRepository's real storage is a plain in-memory List<ClockEntry>. This session studies PayrollDbContext, a new, clearly-labeled extension giving IClockEntryRepository a genuine database-backed alternative implementation.
objectives: Explain the real gap this session fills: the source app's real ClockEntryRepository has no persistence beyond an in-memory list that is discarded when the process exits.
Read PayrollDbContext : DbContext as this codebase's first genuinely framework-required inheritance, previewed in Session 20.
Map ClockEntryEntity's fields to ClockEntry's real properties, and explain why the entity is a separate type rather than reusing ClockEntry directly.
Explain what 'change tracking' means concretely: db.ClockEntries.Add(entity) marks the entity as Added before SaveChangesAsync ever runs.

visuals.title: The real gap: no persistence beyond one process's lifetime
visuals.explanation: ClockEntryRepository's real _clockEntries list exists only in memory -- restarting Parm.Practice.ConsoleApplication loses every clocked-in employee. PayrollDbContext fills this real, unaddressed gap.

visuals.title: PayrollDbContext : DbContext -- required inheritance, not chosen
visuals.explanation: EF Core requires your context type to literally be a DbContext; there is no interface-based alternative for this specific framework capability.

visuals.title: ClockEntryEntity mirrors ClockEntry's shape, but is a distinct type
visuals.explanation: EmployeeId, ClockIn, ClockOut are copied field-for-field from the real ClockEntry -- but ClockEntryEntity is EF Core's storage-shaped type, not the domain's behavior-shaped ClockEntry.

visuals.title: Add marks an entity tracked before anything is saved
visuals.explanation: db.ClockEntries.Add(entity) changes the entity's EntityState to Added immediately -- SaveChangesAsync later translates every tracked change into the actual database write.

preQuiz.prompt: What happens to every ClockEntry the real console app has recorded when the process exits?
options: All of it is lost -- ClockEntryRepository's real storage is an in-memory List<ClockEntry> with no persistence to disk or a database
It is automatically saved to a local file
Nothing -- the real repository already uses EF Core
preQuiz.explanation: This is a real, verified gap in practice-07092026 -- confirmed by reading Repositories/ClockEntryRepository.cs, which has no persistence mechanism at all.

preQuiz.prompt: Why must PayrollDbContext be declared as a class that inherits from DbContext, rather than just implementing an interface?
options: EF Core's design requires your context type to literally extend DbContext to gain its real infrastructure (DbSet<T> properties, change tracking, SaveChangesAsync) -- there is no interface-only way to opt into that machinery
It is a stylistic preference this course chose
preQuiz.explanation: This is the genuinely framework-required inheritance Session 20 previewed -- the first inheritance relationship in this codebase that isn't a deliberate teaching choice.

preQuiz.prompt: What does db.ClockEntries.Add(entity) do before SaveChangesAsync is ever called?
options: It marks the entity as tracked with EntityState.Added -- SaveChangesAsync later reads every tracked entity's state to decide what SQL to generate
It immediately writes the entity to the database
Nothing -- Add has no effect until SaveChangesAsync runs
preQuiz.explanation: Change tracking is exactly this: EF Core records what changed in memory first, then translates the accumulated changes into database operations only when SaveChangesAsync is explicitly called.

concept.title: A real gap, honestly named
paragraphs: Nothing in practice-07092026 persists a ClockEntry anywhere beyond process memory. Every employee's clock-in and clock-out history is gone the moment the console app exits.

This session does not claim EF Core already exists in the real source -- it builds PayrollDbContext specifically because that gap is real, and giving IClockEntryRepository a second, database-backed implementation is the natural next step once the gap is visible.

concept.title: PayrollDbContext: the entity, the context, and change tracking
paragraphs: PayrollDbContext(DbContextOptions<PayrollDbContext> options) : DbContext(options) exposes DbSet<ClockEntryEntity> ClockEntries -- EF Core's queryable, trackable representation of a database table.

ClockEntryEntity deliberately mirrors ClockEntry's real fields (EmployeeId, ClockIn, ClockOut) plus an Id primary key EF Core needs -- it is a separate, storage-shaped type, not a reuse of the domain's ClockEntry class.

concept.title: Why a separate entity, not ClockEntry itself
paragraphs: ClockEntry's real constructor takes only employeeId and clockIn, and ClockOut has a private setter -- both deliberate domain invariants (Session 7-8). EF Core needs to construct and populate ClockEntryEntity freely (including an Id it generates), which would conflict with those same invariants if forced onto ClockEntry directly.
Keeping them separate means ClockEntry's domain rules stay exactly as strict as Sessions 6-25 established, while ClockEntryEntity is free to be exactly as permissive as EF Core's mapping needs.

lab.objective: Trace PayrollDbContext's real shape and confirm change tracking's Added state, using an in-memory SQLite database.
lab.startingCondition: PayrollDbContext and ClockEntryEntity already exist as a new extension in TimeClock.Infrastructure.
steps: Open an in-memory SQLite connection and create a PayrollDbContext against it.
Add a new ClockEntryEntity and check db.Entry(entity).State before calling SaveChangesAsync -- confirm it reports Added.
Call SaveChangesAsync and check db.Entry(entity).State again -- confirm it now reports Unchanged.
Query db.ClockEntries.CountAsync() and confirm exactly one row was persisted.
lab.expectedBehavior: The entity's EntityState transitions from Added to Unchanged exactly when SaveChangesAsync is called; the row count reflects the real, persisted entity afterward.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Confirm PayrollDbContext and ClockEntryEntity's real declarations.
Publish synchronized lesson, lab, and quiz material.

commit: session-31: teach ef core context entities and tracking
review: The real gap (no persistence in the source app) is stated honestly, not assumed away.
PayrollDbContext's inheritance from DbContext is explained as framework-required, connecting back to Session 20's preview.
ClockEntryEntity's separateness from ClockEntry is justified by real, specific domain invariants (constructor shape, private setter), not asserted as a generic best practice.

postQuiz.prompt: If ClockEntryEntity were removed and ClockEntry were used directly as the EF Core entity, what real conflict would arise?
options: EF Core needs to construct ClockEntry objects and assign an Id/ClockOut freely when materializing query results, which conflicts with ClockEntry's real constructor (no Id parameter) and ClockOut's private setter
There would be no conflict -- EF Core can use any class as an entity
ClockEntry would need to become an interface
postQuiz.explanation: This is the concrete, specific reason for the separate entity type -- not a generic 'always separate your layers' rule, but a real conflict between EF Core's needs and ClockEntry's real domain invariants.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does db.Entry(entity).State change from Added to Unchanged only after SaveChangesAsync, not immediately after Add?
options: Add only registers the entity with the context's in-memory change tracker; SaveChangesAsync is the operation that actually executes the database write and then updates tracking to reflect the now-persisted, unchanged state
State never changes -- this is a bug in EF Core
Add and SaveChangesAsync do the same thing
postQuiz.explanation: This two-step behavior -- track first, persist on demand -- is exactly what allows EntryCompletion's validation (Session 25) to run before anything reaches the database (Session 36's workflow).

postQuiz.prompt: Does adding PayrollDbContext change anything about the real, in-memory ClockEntryRepository or its consumers (ClockEntryService, PayrollService)?
options: No -- PayrollDbContext is a new, separate, alternative implementation of persistence; the real ClockEntryRepository and every class depending on IClockEntryRepository continue to work exactly as before
Yes -- ClockEntryRepository is deleted and replaced
postQuiz.explanation: This session adds a new capability alongside the real, unmodified source code -- exactly the 'clearly-labeled extension' framing the task's own instructions call for.

reflections: Why does this session build a new entity type instead of trying to make ClockEntry itself EF Core-compatible?
What would you need to change about PayrollDbContext to make it usable as a real, additional implementation of IClockEntryRepository, alongside the existing in-memory one?
Where else in this codebase might a domain type's strict invariants make it a poor fit for direct use as a persistence entity?
whatBreaks: Constructing ClockEntryEntity with EF Core's usual pattern (a parameterless constructor plus property setters) would fail if attempted against ClockEntry directly, since ClockEntry's real constructor requires employeeId and clockIn and ClockOut cannot be set from outside ClockOutEmployee. Skipping SaveChangesAsync after Add leaves the entity tracked as Added but never actually written to the database -- a common source of 'why didn't my data save' bugs when the two steps are conflated.
summary: The real practice-07092026 source has no persistence beyond an in-memory List<ClockEntry> -- a genuine, verified gap. PayrollDbContext : DbContext is this codebase's first framework-required inheritance (previewed in Session 20), and ClockEntryEntity is a deliberately separate, storage-shaped type -- not a reuse of ClockEntry -- because ClockEntry's real domain invariants (constructor shape, private ClockOut setter) would conflict with how EF Core needs to construct and populate entities.
